Long case 01 · General Surgery

Inguinal Hernia

The most commonly allotted surgical long case, and the one where the examiner is least interested in your diagnosis. He can see the lump. What he wants is the reasoning behind each question you asked and each test you performed.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The case in one breath

S Das defines a hernia as the protrusion of the whole or a part of a viscus through the wall that contains it.​Das 38 · p.594 Bailey & Love puts it as an abnormal protrusion of an organ or tissue through an opening in the layer that normally confines it.​B&L 64 · p.1058 SRB gives the structure that makes the rest of the case easy to organise: every hernia has a covering, a sac, and contents.​SRB 18 · p.741

Two components, and why the defect matters more than the lump B&L reduces every abdominal wall hernia to two essential components: a defect in the wall and the content forced out through it. The weakness is usually the narrowest part, and the hernia expands beyond it into subcutaneous fat. So the nature of the defect, not the size of the swelling, decides the risk: a small defect with rigid walls traps the content and prevents it moving freely in and out.​B&L 64 · p.1060 This single idea explains why a femoral hernia is dangerous and a wide direct hernia is not.
The indirect (oblique, lateral) hernia takes the long route
Out through the deep inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, obliquely along the whole inguinal canal, emerging at the superficial ring.​Das 38 · p.594​B&L 64 · p.1066 It is lateral because its origin is lateral to those vessels, and oblique because it passes from lateral to medial through the muscle layers. Only an indirect hernia can follow the line of the processus vaginalis all the way to the scrotum; a direct hernia cannot.​B&L 64 · p.1066
The direct (medial) hernia takes the short route
Straight through the weak posterior wall at Hesselbach's triangle: inferior epigastric vessels laterally, lateral edge of rectus abdominis medially, inguinal ligament (B&L adds: the iliopubic tract) below. The neck of its sac is therefore medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.​Das 38 · p.603​B&L 64 · p.1066 The weakness exists because here the wall is only transversalis fascia covered by external oblique aponeurosis, with no muscle at all below the arch of the conjoint tendon.​B&L 64 · p.1065, p.1066 B&L adds the line that settles the question in one sentence: a direct hernia is always acquired.​B&L 64 · p.1066
The sac tells you the type before you name it
The neck is narrow in an indirect sac and wide in a direct one. The body is thin in infants, children and indirect sacs, thick in direct and long-standing ones. A hernia with a large mouth may have no neck at all: direct and incisional hernias. An epigastric hernia may have no sac, being a protrusion of extraperitoneal fat.​SRB 18 · p.741 B&L agrees from the other direction: not all abdominal hernias have a peritoneal sac, and many epigastric hernias arise in the interstitial layers, drawing peritoneum in only secondarily once they enlarge.​B&L 64 · p.1058
"Complete" is a defined word
Complete only when the contents reach the bottom of the scrotum. Short of that, incomplete; still inside the superficial ring, a bubonocele.​Das 38 · p.594, p.603
Scale, so you can open with it
Inguinal hernia is the most common hernia in men and is around 10 times more common in men than in women.​B&L 64 · p.1065
The two signs that define it The two classical signs of an uncomplicated hernia are impulse on coughing and reducibility.​Das 38 · p.598 But learn Bailey & Love's two warnings in the same breath, printed as a summary box of their own: a swelling with a cough impulse is not necessarily a hernia, and a swelling with no cough impulse may still be a hernia, though you should then consider other diagnoses.​B&L 64 · p.1061

2Why this patient has a hernia

This is the section where the three books part company, and knowing that is worth marks.

The classical list

SRB gives the list an Indian examiner expects, and its strength is that it stratifies the urinary causes by age:​SRB 18 · p.740–741

Straining and lifting heavy weight
The classical precipitant.
Chronic cough
Tuberculosis, chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, emphysema.
Chronic constipation
Habitual, or from rectal stricture.
Urinary causes, by age
Old age: benign prostatic hyperplasia, carcinoma prostate. Young age: stricture urethra. Very young: phimosis, meatal stenosis.
Obesity, pregnancy, smoking, ascites
Pregnancy and pelvic anatomy matter especially for femoral hernia in women.
Appendicectomy through a McBurney incision
May injure the ilioinguinal nerve, causing a right-sided direct inguinal hernia.​SRB 18 · p.741 S Das makes the same point without naming the nerve.​Das 38 · p.595
A pre-formed sac
Indirect hernia occupies the remains of the processus vaginalis. The chance of a bilateral pre-formed sac is 60%.​SRB 18 · p.741

B&L compresses the same ground into six headings, and it is the cleanest list to recite if you are asked for causes in the abstract: anatomical weakness, developmental failures, genetic weakness of collagen, sharp and blunt trauma, weakness due to ageing and pregnancy, and primary neurological and muscle diseases.​B&L 64 · p.1059

Is a hernia caused by straining? S Das 38 p.594 and SRB 18 p.740 say yes; B&L 64 p.1060 says the strain only reveals it
S Das and SRB
Yes: strenuous work, straining and chronic cough are the causes, acting on an underlying weakness or a persistent processus vaginalis.​Das 38 · p.594​SRB 18 · p.740
Bailey & Love, 28th edition
No. It opens the paragraph with the premise: a normal abdominal wall has sufficient strength to resist high abdominal pressure and prevent herniation, so "many patients will first notice a hernia after excessive straining, the strain bringing the hernia to the attention of the patient, rather than being the cause". The positive case is that hernia is a collagen disease, an inherited imbalance in the types of collagen, supported by histology and by the association with other collagen-related disease such as aortic aneurysm. In extreme collagen disorders, such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, durable repair is very difficult. Even the smoking association is routed through collagen: hernia is more common in smokers because smoking impairs collagen maturation.​B&L 64 · p.1060
How to answer: give the classical list, then add that modern evidence treats raised pressure as the event that reveals a hernia rather than the cause of it, the underlying defect being collagen. SRB itself supports this, calling acquired herniation a collagen deficiency, what it names "metastatic emphysema of Read".​SRB 18 · p.741 Connecting the two books is what separates a good answer from a recited one.

Edition note. If you have heard the line that hernia is "no more common in Olympic weightlifters than in the general population", that was the 26th edition's way of making this argument. The 28th edition has removed it and argues the same conclusion from collagen biology, Ehlers–Danlos and the smoking link instead. Quote the mechanism, not the weightlifters.
Does obesity cause inguinal hernia? SRB 18 p.740 lists it; B&L 64 p.1060 ties high BMI only to incisional hernia
SRB
Lists obesity among the causes of inguinal hernia.​SRB 18 · p.740
Bailey & Love, 28th edition
Does not. Where it discusses body habitus it says incisional hernias are more common after wound complications and in patients with a high body mass index, and that a major risk factor is the surgeon and the way the abdominal wall was closed.​B&L 64 · p.1060 For inguinal hernia it offers shape rather than weight: risk is greater in patients with a wider and shorter pelvis.​B&L 64 · p.1059
How to answer: list obesity, because it is in the Indian text and the examiner is working from that list, but place it correctly: the evidence for a high BMI is strong for incisional hernia and weak for inguinal hernia. If you want a risk factor for inguinal hernia that B&L will back you on, say pelvic shape.

Edition note. The 26th edition went further and reported a Swedish study finding inguinal hernia less common in obese patients, risk negatively related to BMI, "contrary to widespread belief". The 28th edition has dropped that claim entirely. Do not quote it as current Bailey & Love teaching.

What Bailey & Love adds that the others do not

The only natural weaknesses
Despite the complexity of the abdominal wall, the only weaknesses from inadequate muscular strength are the lumbar triangles and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Structures passing through create the rest
The commonest example is the inguinal canal, through which the testis descends in the male and the round ligament passes in the female. Other inherent weak points are the oesophageal hiatus, the femoral canal and the umbilical cicatrix.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Hormonal control of processus closure
Calcitonin gene-related peptide and hepatocyte growth factor influence closure of the processus, raising the possibility of a hormonal cause of hernia development.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Why scars herniate
A surgical scar, even with perfect wound healing, has only 70% of the initial muscle strength, giving incisional herniation in at least 10% of laparotomy incisions. Laparoscopic port sites, 1%: so wider use of laparoscopy should make incisional hernia less common.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Pelvic shape
Risk is higher in patients with a wider and shorter pelvis.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Ageing
More common in the elderly from degenerative weakness of muscle and fibrous tissue.​B&L 64 · p.1060
Divarication is not a hernia
The linea alba stretches laterally as the recti separate: in the upper abdomen in middle-aged overweight men, and below the umbilicus in women after pregnancy. B&L says plainly that divarication is not a hernia and does not require treatment, though some surgeons repair it for cosmesis.​B&L 64 · p.1058
The mechanism of strangulation, in one paragraph Trapped tissue sits in a confined space. The narrow neck acts as a constriction ring, impeding venous return and raising pressure inside the hernia; the resulting tension causes pain and tenderness. If bowel is present it obstructs, partially or totally. If pressure rises enough that arterial blood cannot enter, the contents become ischaemic and may infarct. The hernia has strangulated, and the bowel wall then perforates, releasing infected toxic content into the tissues and ultimately back into the peritoneal cavity. Risk is highest where the neck is small and rigid, leading first to irreducibility and on to strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1060 This is why "small hernias can be more dangerous than large".​B&L 64 · p.1062
One word the Indian books do not use Incarcerated, literally "in prison", means in B&L that a hernia is not only irreducible but also potentially developing strangulation. It is the stage between the two and it has its own line in B&L's classification by complexity.​B&L 64 · p.1060 S Das and SRB do not use it as a separate type, so if an examiner uses the word, define it before you answer.

3History, and why each question earns its place

Particulars

Age? WhyIndirect hernia is usually met with in young individuals; direct hernia mostly in older subjects, and more common above 40.​Das 38 · p.594, p.604 B&L agrees: a direct, medial hernia is more likely in elderly patients, and inguinal hernia in neonates and children is always the congenital type.​B&L 64 · p.1066
CarefulA congenital hernia, meaning one occupying a pre-formed sac, is usually seen in adults, despite the name.​Das 38 · p.603 B&L explains why: the muscles around the deep ring can hold a patent processus closed until later in life, when constant positive abdominal pressure stretches ring and muscle and the hernia finally appears.​B&L 64 · p.1066
Occupation? WhyStrenuous work precipitates herniation against a background of weak muscle or a persistent processus vaginalis.​Das 38 · p.594 The load is the trigger; the anatomy is the permission. And see the disagreement above: B&L would call the load the moment of discovery rather than the cause.

The complaint

Is there pain? What kind, and when in the day is it worst? WhyEarly, with only a "tendency to hernia", the pain is dragging and aching, worse as the day passes. It may appear long before the lump, continues while the hernia is progressing, and ceases once the hernia is fully formed.​Das 38 · p.594
SoA patient whose pain has settled is not improving. His hernia has finished forming.
B&L's gradingUsually painless, or an aching or heavy feeling. Sharp, intermittent pains suggest pinching of tissue at the hernia neck. Severe pain should alert you to a high risk of strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1061
Rules outB&L's corollary, which matters when pain is the main complaint: soft, reducible hernias are rarely painful. So if the hernia is soft and reduces easily and the pain is severe, be certain the pain is actually coming from the hernia and not from coexisting pathology.​B&L 64 · p.1061
Has it become suddenly very painful and tender? Rules inStrangulation. The patient may complain of pain all over the abdomen from drag on the mesentery or omentum.​Das 38 · p.594 This is the answer that converts the case from elective to emergency, and B&L's management rule follows directly: acute pain in a hernia, particularly if it is irreducible, means urgent surgery.​B&L 64 · p.1062

The four set questions for any inguinoscrotal swelling

Asked in this order for every groin swelling; each eliminates something specific.​Das 38 · p.594–595

1. How did it start: on straining, coughing, or lifting? Rules inHernia; onset on straining is the usual story.
Rules outA swelling with no straining event moves you towards the differential list: a hydrocele, a lipoma of the cord, a lymph node.
2. Where did it first appear? DistinguishesInguinal from femoral, by direction of travel. Groin descending into the scrotum → inguinal. Below the groin crease, ascending → femoral.
Why it beats palpationA large femoral hernia eventually climbs above the inguinal ligament and will mislead your hand.​Das 38 · p.597 B&L says the same: as it enlarges it is reflected superiorly and becomes difficult to distinguish from a medial direct hernia arising only a few centimetres above the femoral canal.​B&L 64 · p.1071
3. What was its size and extent when first noticed? DistinguishesCongenital from acquired. Bottom of the scrotum at first appearance → a pre-formed sac, congenital. Acquired starts small, enlarges gradually, and does not become complete at once.​Das 38 · p.595, p.603
4. Does it disappear automatically on lying down? DistinguishesDirect from indirect before you touch the patient. Direct disappears as soon as he lies down. Indirect has to be reduced, and once reduced needs a cough to bring it back.​Das 38 · p.595, p.603 B&L's version of the same question is a management one: determine whether the hernia reduces spontaneously or has to be helped, because that is the first step on the scale that ends in strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1061

Systemic symptoms

Colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation? Rules inThe four cardinal symptoms of intestinal obstruction, so this is an obstructed hernia.​Das 38 · p.595 B&L makes it an explicit instruction: the patient should be asked about symptoms that might suggest bowel obstruction.​B&L 64 · p.1061
ButObstruction may be absent in omentocele, Richter's hernia and Littre's hernia, so its absence does not exclude strangulation.​SRB 18 · p.743​Das 38 · p.605 B&L says it of Richter's in as many words: bowel obstruction may or may not be present, yet the bowel wall can still become necrotic and perforate with life-threatening consequences.​B&L 64 · p.1060
If vomiting: what does the vomitus smell like? WhyBilious or faecal. Faecal smelling vomitus heralds an ominous sign.​Das 38 · p.595 Asking about the character, not merely the presence, is the difference between a student and a clinician.

Hunting the cause: the questions the patient will not volunteer

Why this section decides the operation The patient deliberately does not mention cough, constipation and bladder symptoms, considering them irrelevant, and S Das gives explicit permission to use leading questions to extract them.​Das 38 · p.595 Miss them and the patient returns with a recurrence.​Das 1 · p.8
Persistent cough? Chronic bronchitis? Smoking? Tuberculosis, asthma, emphysema? WhyA repeated pressure load on the repair, and a cause of recurrence.​Das 38 · p.595​SRB 18 · p.740
B&L's extra reasonSmoking is independently associated, and the stated mechanism is impaired collagen maturation, not the cough. So the advice to stop smoking before a repair is about the healing of the repair, not only about the pressure on it.​B&L 64 · p.1060
Constipation: do you strain at stool? WhySame mechanism, and the reason rectal examination later becomes obligatory.​Das 38 · p.602–603 Ask about rectal stricture as well as habit.​SRB 18 · p.740
Frequency, urgency, poor stream, hesitancy, terminal dribbling? Rules inProstatic enlargement, or a urethral stricture.​Das 38 · p.595 Stratify by age: BPH or carcinoma prostate in the old, stricture in the young, phimosis or meatal stenosis in the very young.​SRB 18 · p.740
SoTreated before or alongside the repair, or the straining continues and so does the recurrence risk.​Das 38 · p.603
AndFlag it to the anaesthetist. Urinary retention is one of B&L's listed immediate complications of inguinal hernia surgery and may require catheterisation.​B&L 64 · p.1070
Does the swelling get bigger just before you pass urine, and smaller after? Rules inA cystocele. Pressure on it induces a desire to micturate. Occurs only in a direct or sliding hernia.​Das 38 · p.604 B&L confirms the mechanism twice over: extraperitoneal content alone can fill a hernia, urinary bladder in a direct inguinal hernia being its own example, and the bladder can be pulled into a direct hernia, shown on a cystogram.​B&L 64 · p.1060, p.1066

Past, drug and systems history

Any previous abdominal operation, especially appendicectomy? WhyDivision of the ilioinguinal nerve at a McBurney incision weakens the inguinal region and produces a subsequent right-sided direct hernia.​SRB 18 · p.741​Das 38 · p.595 A right iliac fossa scar with a right direct hernia is a causal chain you can state.
Any previous hernia repair: which side? DistinguishesSame side → recurrent hernia. B&L makes this one of the three things to establish once you are satisfied the swelling is a hernia at all: is it primary, recurrent, or incisional? Recurrent and incisional hernias are more difficult to treat and may require a different surgical approach.​B&L 64 · p.1061 Opposite side → expected, since a right hernia generally precedes a left.​Das 38 · p.595
SoA recurrence after failed open repair is one of the two situations where B&L says the laparoscopic approach is of particular benefit.​B&L 64 · p.1069
Are you on warfarin, apixaban, aspirin or clopidogrel? Any cardiac or respiratory disease? WhyB&L names the drugs: anticoagulants such as warfarin and apixaban and antiplatelet agents such as aspirin and clopidogrel, because they impact on future surgery. General cardiac and respiratory questions assess anaesthetic risk.​B&L 64 · p.1061
Also askHome support, distance from hospital and mobility, because many hernia operations are a day case or single overnight stay and the patient has to be suitable for that.​B&L 64 · p.1061 It is the one history question that is purely about logistics, and examiners like it because nobody remembers it.

4Examination, and what each finding settles

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.

This one is intimate, so the chaperone is not a courtesy B&L's wording is "especially for intimate examinations", and it adds that this "should be part of a local guideline or policy".​B&L 21 · p.285 Offer a chaperone whatever your sex and the patient's, say that you have offered, and say you would record it. For a child, explain it to the child and ask the parent. If consent is refused, say that you would explain again, offer a chaperone, document the refusal, and not proceed. Examiners ask what you would do if she declined, and that is the whole answer.
Standing first, or lying first? S Das 38 p.596 says standing; B&L 64 p.1061 says lying
S Das
Standing first, then supine. Inguinal, femoral, epigastric, obturator, lumbar, gluteal and Spigelian herniae are all best examined standing, and the standing examination "should not be omitted". The patient holds his clothes up and must not bend forward.​Das 38 · p.596
Bailey & Love
Lying down initially and then standing, "as this will usually increase hernia size". Some hernias will only be apparent standing. The patient may be asked to cough or to perform the Valsalva manoeuvre to make the hernia appear.​B&L 64 · p.1061
How to answer: they are after different things. S Das wants the hernia demonstrated, which gravity does. B&L wants it reduced and assessed, which lying does, and then confirms it standing. Examine standing first so you do not miss a direct hernia that vanishes supine, then lie the patient down to reduce it and assess the defect, then stand him again to confirm. Say that reasoning aloud and the discrepancy becomes a strength. Note also that it is B&L, not the Indian texts, that offers you the Valsalva manoeuvre as an alternative to coughing: useful in a patient who cannot cough to order.

Before you begin

Expose both inguinal regions, umbilicus to mid-thigh
Both sides: the opposite groin is part of the examination, not a courtesy.​Das 38 · p.595 B&L makes it a rule for groin hernia: if a groin hernia is found on one side, the other side must also be examined, because occult contralateral hernias are present in up to 20% of patients.​B&L 64 · p.1061 And for femoral hernia, inadequate exposure of this area during routine examination is why the hernia is missed.​B&L 64 · p.1071
B&L's checklist, which is a printed summary box
Reducibility; cough impulse; tenderness; overlying skin colour changes; multiple defects and the contralateral side; signs of previous repair; scrotal content for a groin hernia; associated pathology.​B&L 64 · p.1061 Recite it as a list and nothing gets left out.

Inspection

Pyriform, with a stalk at the external ring, extending into the scrotum
Indirect.​Das 38 · p.596
Spherical, little tendency to enter the scrotum
Direct. B&L adds the two facts that follow from its shape: it is broadly based and therefore unlikely to strangulate, and it cannot reach the bottom of the scrotum because it does not follow the processus vaginalis.​Das 38 · p.596​B&L 64 · p.1066
Spherical, arising below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Femoral. Narrow in the canal, expanding once through the saphenous opening into the retort shape.​Das 38 · p.596, p.606 B&L's description is the same and adds where to look: it lies in the upper leg rather than in the lower abdomen.​B&L 64 · p.1071
Extent to the bottom of the scrotum
Congenital. Stopping just above the testis: funicular or acquired.​Das 38 · p.596
Visible peristalsis
Possible when the covering is thin, as in recurrent hernia. Never in femoral hernia. Do not mistake dartos contraction of scrotal skin for it.​Das 38 · p.596
Skin red, or overlying cellulitis
Strangulation or inflamed hernia. B&L is unambiguous: if there is overlying cellulitis then the hernia content is strangulating and the case should be treated as an emergency.​Das 38 · p.596​B&L 64 · p.1061
Brown streaky pigmentation, wrinkled atrophic skin
Long-term truss use with haemosiderin deposition.​Das 38 · p.596 Worth knowing that B&L now says surgical trusses are not recommended and few surgeons advise them.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1068 So this sign is becoming a historical one, but it still appears in Indian wards.
Wide, irregular, puckered scar
Wound infection after previous surgery: a common cause of recurrence.​Das 38 · p.596
Penis pushed to the opposite side
A large inguinal hernia.​Das 38 · p.597

Cough impulse

Ask the patient to turn his face away, then cough. Watch, then feel. Why turn the faceTo avoid the salivary shower.​Das 38 · p.596 Say it: examiners notice.
Rules inAn expansile impulse is almost diagnostic of a hernia.​Das 38 · p.596–597 B&L's technique: gentle pressure applied to the lump while the patient coughs.​B&L 64 · p.1061
Does not rule outAbsent if the neck is blocked by adhesions.​Das 38 · p.597 B&L gives the general rule: there may be no cough impulse when the neck is tight and the hernia irreducible. This is typical of a femoral hernia, where the lack of an impulse leads the clinician to misdiagnose a lymph node.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1071
False positiveA saphena varix also gives a definite cough impulse, increases on standing, and is misdiagnosed as a hernia, particularly in pregnant women.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1067
Nothing found at all?B&L's closing instruction on examination: if a patient describes an intermittent swelling but the surgeon finds no hernia, there still may be a hernia present. Surgeons often accept the diagnosis on history alone, or re-examine later, or request an ultrasound.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1067

Palpation

Edition note, not a live disagreement: medial or lateral to the pubic tubercle? The books now agree. S Das 38 p.597 says medial; B&L said lateral in 26e and has deleted the sentence in 28e
S Das
An inguinal hernia lies above the inguinal ligament and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia below the ligament and lateral to the tubercle.​Das 38 · p.597
Bailey & Love, 28th edition
Makes no statement at all about where an inguinal hernia sits relative to the pubic tubercle. The only relation it prints is the femoral one, and it matches S Das: the femoral hernia appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.​B&L 64 · p.1071 Its one statement about an inguinal hernia and a bony landmark is in a figure caption: a right direct inguinal hernia defect is above the inguinal ligament.​B&L 64 · p.1059
Nothing to reconcile here: answer S Das and move on. Above-and-medial for inguinal, below-and-lateral for femoral is the classical relation your examiner expects, it is the one that works at the bedside, and in the 28th edition Bailey & Love no longer contradicts it. This box is in the guide only because the old wording is still in circulation, so treat it as history rather than as a question with two defensible answers.

What changed. The 26th edition described the inguinal hernia as lying "above and lateral to the pubic tubercle", which is why some seniors and some notes still teach it that way. That sentence is gone from the 28th edition. If an examiner quotes it at you, you may say, politely, that the current edition does not make that claim and that the femoral relation it does give is below and lateral. Knowing where a line came from is worth more than knowing the line.
Cannot "get above" the swelling
Inguinoscrotal: a hernia. In a pure scrotal swelling you can get above it and feel only cord structures. Useless in femoral hernia, which produces no scrotal swelling.​Das 38 · p.597–598 B&L frames it the same way and makes it the way out of a specific trap: large scrotal hernias are misdiagnosed as a hydrocele or other testicular swelling, but a large scrotal hernia has no upper limit because it extends back along the inguinal canal to the peritoneal cavity.​B&L 64 · p.1067
Elastic consistency
Enterocele.​Das 38 · p.598
Doughy and granular
Omentocele / epiplocele.​Das 38 · p.598
Tense and tender
Strangulated: of great importance in making this diagnosis.​Das 38 · p.598 It is also two of the four items on B&L's high-risk list: pain, tenderness, skin changes and difficulty reducing imply a high risk of strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1062
Relation to testis and cord
An inguinal hernia lies in front of and to the sides of the cord and testis. If acquired or funicular it stops above the testis, so the testis is felt separately.​Das 38 · p.598
Obese patient, tubercle impalpable
Trace the tendon of adductor longus upwards to reach it.​Das 38 · p.597

The special tests

Where is the deep inguinal ring? S Das 38 p.599 and SRB 18 p.743 give one landmark; B&L 64 p.1065 another
S Das
½ inch above the mid-inguinal point: the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the symphysis pubis.​Das 38 · p.599
SRB
1.25 cm above the inguinal ligament, midway between the symphysis pubis and the ASIS: the same landmark as S Das.​SRB 18 · p.743
Bailey & Love, 28th edition
Unchanged from the 26th, and now phrased in a way that makes the distinction impossible to miss: the deep ring "lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 2–3 cm above and marginally lateral to the femoral artery pulse".​B&L 64 · p.1065 At operation it repeats the point: once the hernia is reduced, locate the deep ring just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.​B&L 64 · p.1067
Both landmarks are real and they are about 1–1.5 cm apart. The mid-inguinal point (ASIS to symphysis pubis) overlies the femoral artery. The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle) overlies the deep inguinal ring. B&L's own wording proves it: it places the ring lateral to the femoral artery pulse, which is exactly where the mid-inguinal point is not. Modern anatomy favours B&L. Indian textbooks and most examiners will expect the S Das wording. Give the S Das answer, and if pressed, state the distinction between the two points. It is one of the most reliable ways to show you have read more than one book.

Zieman's technique: which hernia is it?

Three fingers, three rings. Then the patient holds his nose and blows, which Zieman preferred, or coughs. IndexOn the deep ring. Impulse → indirect.
MiddleOn the superficial ring. Impulse → direct.
Ring fingerOn the saphenous opening, 4 cm (1½ inches) below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Impulse → femoral.​Das 38 · p.599, p.606
PreconditionOnly when there is no obvious swelling, or after complete reduction.​Das 38 · p.599
HonestyThis is one of the "other examination techniques" B&L alludes to before saying that even experienced surgeons cannot reliably separate lateral from medial hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1067 Perform it, report it, do not over-claim it.

Invagination test

After reduction, recumbent. Little finger, invaginating scrotal skin from the bottom, up to the pubic tubercle, then rotate into the superficial ring. Right hand for the right side. Why the little fingerTo minimise hurting the patient; utmost gentleness.​Das 38 · p.600
Normal ringA triangular slit admitting only the fingertip. SRB: the superficial ring is a triangular opening 1.25 cm above the pubic tubercle, bounded by a superomedial and an inferolateral crus, which normally does not, or only just, admits the tip of the little finger.​SRB 18 · p.743​Das 38 · p.600 B&L gives the anatomy behind the shape: the testis emerges through an inverted V-shaped defect in the external oblique aponeurosis.​B&L 64 · p.1065
DirectionDirectly backwards → direct. Upwards, backwards and outwards → indirect. Impulse on the pulp → direct; on the tip → oblique.​Das 38 · p.600–601

Ring occlusion test

Hernia reduced. Thumb or finger over the deep ring, then cough. LogicAn indirect hernia emerges through the ring; a direct one medial to it.
Rules inBulge medial to the occluding finger → direct. No bulge → indirect.​Das 38 · p.601 B&L describes the identical manoeuvre as its primary bedside test, and spells out the sequence: reduce the hernia, identify ASIS and pubic tubercle, find the deep ring just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, apply gentle pressure there, ask the patient to cough. Controlled by the pressure → indirect / lateral. Appearing medial to that point despite the pressure → direct / medial.​B&L 64 · p.1067
Honesty requiredB&L adds that even experienced surgeons find it difficult to distinguish lateral and medial hernias with certainty.​B&L 64 · p.1067 If an examiner asks how confident you are, that is the answer, and the final distinction is made at operation.

Reducibility and Taxis

Lie the patient down. Flex, adduct and internally rotate the thigh. Hold the fundus, apply even pressure, guide the contents through the superficial ring. Why that positionIt relaxes the pillars of the superficial ring and the oblique muscles.​Das 38 · p.600
Let the patient try firstB&L: if the hernia does not reduce spontaneously, ask the patient to attempt reduction, because he may be well practised in the task while the surgeon might cause unnecessary discomfort. If neither can reduce it, the treatment is more urgent.​B&L 64 · p.1061
WarningTaxis must be very gentle. Rough handling will bring forth fatal complications.​Das 38 · p.600
GurgleEnterocele: first part difficult, last part slips in easily. Omentocele: first part easy, last part resists.​Das 38 · p.600, p.604​SRB 18 · p.742
After reductionAssess the size, rigidity and number of defects: multiple defects occur in incisional hernia, and the rigidity is what predicts strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1060, p.1061
Is taxis ever allowed on an irreducible, painful hernia? S Das 38 p.600 forbids force; B&L 64 p.1062 permits "gentle forceful reduction"
S Das
Taxis is for a reducible hernia and must be very gentle; rough handling will bring forth fatal complications. The classical teaching that follows is that taxis is contraindicated in a strangulated hernia, because reducing dead bowel returns it to the abdomen where the perforation goes unwitnessed.​Das 38 · p.600 SRB supplies the consequence by name: Garrey's stricture, an ischaemic narrowing found later at operation in bowel that was reduced from an obstructed hernia.​SRB 18 · p.742–743
Bailey & Love, 28th edition
Explicitly allows it, and defines the term in the parenthesis: a patient with acute pain in a hernia, particularly if irreducible, should be offered urgent surgery, but "it may be reducible by taxis (gentle forceful reduction, perhaps requiring analgesia and/or sedation)", and sometimes, after admission and adequate analgesia, the hernia will reduce as a result of muscle relaxation. Either way the likelihood of a repeat episode is very high, so surgery is recommended at the next available opportunity.​B&L 64 · p.1062
How to answer: state the classical rule as your own position: do not attempt taxis on a tense, tender hernia with features of strangulation. Then separate the two situations, because that is what resolves the disagreement. An irreducible but not strangulated hernia may be reduced under analgesia in hospital, which is what B&L means, and it earns the patient an operation on the next list rather than at midnight. A strangulated hernia is never reduced blindly: it is resuscitated and explored, because the bowel has to be seen. If you are asked for the hazard of getting this wrong, name Garrey's stricture and the unwitnessed perforation.

Percussion, auscultation and the rest

Resonant
Enterocele: and it separates a strangulated hernia (resonant) from acute epididymitis and acute filarial funiculitis (both dull).​Das 38 · p.601–602
Dull
Omentum or extraperitoneal fat.​Das 38 · p.601–602
Auscultation
Little diagnostic value; peristaltic sounds over an enterocele.​Das 38 · p.602
Traction test
Pulling the testis down makes an encysted hydrocele of the cord descend slightly and become fixed.​Das 38 · p.601–602
Scrotal contents
B&L calls it essential in men: to exclude other pathology and to check that the patient has both testes.​B&L 64 · p.1067 It is also one line of the examination summary box.​B&L 64 · p.1061

Tone of the abdominal muscles: the finding that chooses the operation

Why bother Tone is examined to select the operation: herniorrhaphy or hernioplasty.​Das 38 · p.602; ch.1 · p.8 It is the clearest case in the whole examination of a sign that directly decides management, and it maps onto what B&L calls the tailored approach: no one operation suits all hernias, and the surgeon's skills, the equipment, the patient and the hernia's characteristics together decide which repair, or indeed whether no operation at all is the best management plan.​B&L 64 · p.1069
In profile: undue protrusion of the lower abdomen
Loss of tone.​Das 38 · p.602
Rising test: supine, raise the shoulders against resistance
Strong obliques retract the wall over the flanks. Weak muscles reveal Malgaigne's bulgings: oval, longitudinal, bilateral bulges above and parallel to the medial half of the inguinal ligament.​Das 38 · p.602
Finger in the superficial ring during a cough
Assesses the two pillars and the sphincteric action of the conjoined tendon.​Das 38 · p.602
Divarification of the recti
Best seen by asking a supine patient simply to lift his head off the pillow.​B&L 64 · p.1061 It is the linea alba stretching laterally as the recti separate: in the upper abdomen in middle-aged overweight men, and below the umbilicus as a result of pregnancy in women. Remember to say that it is not a hernia and needs no treatment, or you will be asked how you would repair it.​B&L 64 · p.1058

General examination: four jobs, not a ritual

S Das sets out why a general examination is done at all: for diagnosis and differential diagnosis, to select the anaesthetic, to determine the nature of the operation, and to determine prognosis.​Das 1 · p.8 In hernia the third is the one that matters.

Chest, thoroughly
To exclude any cause of chronic cough.​Das 38 · p.602–603
Rectal examination: obligatory
To exclude chronic constipation and an enlarged prostate. The word in the text is obligatory.​Das 38 · p.603
Abdomen
Always, to exclude intestinal obstruction.​Das 38 · p.603
The opposite groin
A right hernia generally precedes a left.​Das 38 · p.595 B&L quantifies it: occult contralateral hernias in up to 20% of patients, and a patient with a single hernia has a 50% lifetime risk of developing one on the other side.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1067
A figure that changed between editions If you have learned the contralateral lifetime risk as 33%, that was the 26th edition. The 28th edition says 50%.​B&L 64 · p.1067 Quote 50% and attribute it; if the examiner has the older figure, the fact that you know both is the answer.

Differential diagnosis of a groin swelling

SRB's list is the one to reproduce, grouped by tissue of origin:​SRB 18 · p.741

GroupSwellings
IntegumentSebaceous cyst, lipoma, neurofibroma
HerniaInguinal, femoral
LymphaticInguinal lymphadenopathy
VascularSaphena varix, aneurysm
Inguinal canalEctopic testis, lipoma or hydrocele of the cord, hydrocele of the canal of Nuck (female)
DeepPsoas abscess

The common four are inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, inguinal lymphadenopathy and saphena varix. Groin pain may be hernia, funiculitis, varicocele, lymph node disease or post-surgical pain.​SRB 18 · p.741

B&L's two lists, which are differently organised and worth having as well
For an irreducible, tense inguinal hernia with no cough impulse: groin lymph node mass, psoas abscess, subcutaneous soft tissue mass such as a lipoma, or an abdominal mass.​B&L 64 · p.1067 For a femoral hernia, as a printed summary box: inguinal hernia, lymph node, saphena varix, femoral artery aneurysm, psoas abscess and rupture of adductor longus with haematoma.​B&L 64 · p.1071 The last one is the item nobody else lists; it is worth a mark on its own.

5The anatomy, which is the question you are most likely to be asked

Every one of these is a stock viva question on this case, and all of it is in SRB's hernia chapter. An examiner who has watched you examine the groin will almost always follow with "tell me the boundaries of the inguinal canal" or "what are the coverings of the sac". None of it can be reasoned out at the bedside; it has to be known.

Boundaries of the inguinal canal
SRB gives the four walls, and this is the wording to learn: "In front: external oblique aponeurosis and conjoined muscle laterally. Behind: inferior epigastric artery, fascia transversalis and conjoined tendon medially. Above: conjoined muscle (arched fibres of internal oblique). Below: inguinal ligament."​SRB 18 · p.744
Say it in order, front, back, above, belowFour walls, four answers. The two that carry the marks are behind, because that is where a direct hernia comes through and where the repair is done, and below, because the inguinal ligament is the landmark that separates this hernia from a femoral one.
What keeps a hernia out, and why this canal normally holds
SRB lists five mechanisms, and an examiner asking "why does everyone not have a hernia" wants them: "obliquity of inguinal canal; arching of conjoint tendon; 'shutter mechanism' of internal oblique; 'ball valve mechanism' due to contraction of cremaster muscle which plugs to superficial ring; when external oblique muscle contracts, intercrural fibres of superficial ring appose causing 'slit valve mechanism'."​SRB 18 · p.744
This is also the answer to a question about causesThe section on why this patient has a hernia asks exactly that. These five are why most patients do not, so anything that defeats them — a wide or straight canal, a weak or scarred internal oblique, a persistently raised intra-abdominal pressure — is the mechanism of the hernia you are standing in front of.
Coverings of an indirect inguinal hernia
An indirect sac leaves through the deep ring with the cord, so it picks up the cord's own coverings in order. SRB names them from the inside out: "internal spermatic fascia from fascia transversalis. Cremasteric fascia. External spermatic fascia from external oblique aponeurosis is seen below the external ring in the scrotum."​SRB 18 · p.744 And the scrotal wall it then lies within: "1. skin 2. dartos muscle 3. external spermatic fascia 4. cremasteric fascia 5. internal spermatic fascia."​SRB 26 · p.1056
So, from the skin inwardsSkin, dartos, external spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric fascia (from internal oblique), internal spermatic fascia (from fascia transversalis), then extraperitoneal fat, then the sac itself, which is peritoneum. Each layer is named after the muscle it comes from, which is the way to remember it rather than a list: the sac picks up a coat from every layer it pushes through.
Contents of the spermatic cord
SRB's figure names them: vas deferens, artery of the ductus deferens, pampiniform plexus of veins, the artery to the cremaster, the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, the ilioinguinal nerve and lymph vessels.​SRB 18 · p.744
Note where the ilioinguinal nerve isSRB draws it on the cord rather than within it, and that is the nerve at risk in the operation. It is the reason numbness over the scrotum and the medial thigh is a recognised complication of a repair, and an examiner who asks which nerve you would avoid is asking about this one.
Direct against indirect, in the terms the books define them
SRB: the indirect hernia "comes out through internal ring along with the cord. It is lateral to the inferior epigastric artery." The direct hernia "occurs through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal through 'Hesselbach's triangle'... Sac is medial to the inferior epigastric artery."​SRB 18 · p.745
Hesselbach's triangle, which is the direct hernia's doorway SRB bounds it: "medially by lateral border of rectus muscle, laterally by inferior epigastric artery, below by inguinal ligament."​SRB 18 · p.745
One artery settles bothThe inferior epigastric artery is the whole distinction: lateral to it is indirect, medial to it is direct. Every other difference follows from that one fact, which is why it is the sentence to lead with.
 IndirectDirect
RouteThrough the deep ring, along the canal, with the cord Straight through the posterior wall, through Hesselbach's triangle
Relation to the inferior epigastric arteryLateral Medial
Relation to the cordWithin the coverings, with the cord Pushes the cord aside; not within its coverings
Shape and descentOblique; may reach the scrotum Globular; rarely reaches the scrotum
Ring occlusion testControlled by pressure over the deep ring Not controlled; it reappears
Typical ageAny age, commonest in the young Older, with a weak posterior wall
Risk of strangulationHigher, because the neck is narrow Low, because the neck is wide

The first two rows are SRB's definitions, p.745. The rest are drawn from the signs and tests in the examination section above and from the strangulation reasoning under treatment, gathered here because the question is always asked as a table. Remember what the examination section says before you recite it: even experienced surgeons cannot reliably separate direct from indirect at the bedside, so the table is how the two differ, not a claim that you can always tell which you are feeling.

How far the sac has come, which is a separate classification
SRB: "Incomplete: bubonocele: here sac is confined to the inguinal canal. Funicular: here sac crosses the superficial inguinal ring, but does not reach the bottom of the scrotum. Complete: here sac descends to the bottom of the scrotum." And the one with two limbs: "saddle-bag or pantaloon hernial sac has got both medial and lateral component."​SRB 18 · p.745
Use the word for what you foundSaying "a complete indirect inguinal hernia" tells the examiner the sac reaches the bottom of the scrotum and that you know the term for it. Bubonocele and funicular are the two that candidates forget.
And the landmark that separates inguinal from femoral
SRB states it as a note, and it is the single most useful line in the groin: "inguinal hernia is above and medial to the pubic tubercle. Femoral hernia is below and lateral to pubic tubercle."​SRB 18 · p.745
Find the tubercle before you decideThis is only as good as your finger on the pubic tubercle, which is why the examination section spends so long on finding it. Get the landmark wrong and the sentence gives you the wrong hernia with complete confidence.

6Classifying what you found

Anatomical

AxisTypes
By extent Bubonocele: not out of the superficial ring · Incomplete: out of the ring, not to the bottom of the scrotum · Complete: reaches the bottom of the scrotum
By site of exit Oblique / indirect / lateral: through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels · Direct / medial: through Hesselbach's triangle, neck medial to the vessels
By content Enterocele · Epiplocele / omentocele · Cystocele · Littre's (Meckel's) · Richter's (part of bowel wall) · Amyand's (appendix) · ovary with fallopian tube · fluid

Extent and exit: S Das ch.38 p.603. Contents list: SRB ch.18 p.741–742.

Clinical types

S Das gives five; SRB gives six, adding occult; B&L classifies by complexity and gives six of its own, inserting incarcerated and ending at infarcted. Learn SRB's six and know where B&L's scale ends.​Das 38 · p.604–605​SRB 18 · p.742–743​B&L 64 · p.1060

TypeDefinitionHow you tell
Occult Not detectable clinically. Groin pain with no palpable swelling and possibly no expansile impulse.
Reducible Contents return; the sac stays. B&L: "a swelling that appears and disappears". Expansile impulse present. Intestine reduces with a gurgle, first portion hardest; omentum doughy, last portion hardest.
Irreducible Contents will not return; nothing else wrong. Not tender, not tense, skin normal. Causes: narrow neck, adhesions, overcrowding, sliding hernia, very large scrotal hernia. Predisposes to strangulation.
Incarcerated
(B&L only)		 Irreducible, trapped, potentially developing strangulation. The stage between irreducible and strangulated. Not a separate type in S Das or SRB.
Obstructed
(Indian texts)		 Irreducible + obstruction. Blood supply intact. Shares two features with strangulation. Eventually leads to it.
Inflamed Contents inflamed: appendicitis, salpingitis. Tender but not tense; skin red and oedematous; no obstruction.
Strangulated Irreducible + obstruction + arrested blood supply. Tense, tender, no impulse on coughing, features of obstruction. B&L: "acutely painful swelling with tissue ischaemia: requires emergency surgery".
Infarcted
(B&L only)		 Contents have become gangrenous. High mortality. The far end of the scale, and the reason the whole scale is worth learning.

B&L's six, in its own order: occult, reducible, irreducible, incarcerated, strangulated, infarcted. Summary box 64.2, ch.64 p.1060.

The strangulation question, answered properly The most common strangulated hernia is the indirect inguinal hernia, because inguinal hernias are so much more numerous. The highest rate of strangulation is in the femoral hernia, as a proportion of femoral hernias.​SRB 18 · p.743 Students who have only read one book give one of these and get caught by the other. B&L adds the scale: 50% of femoral hernias present as an emergency,​B&L 64 · p.1071 while only about 5% of inguinal hernias present as an irreducible painful lump.​B&L 64 · p.1070
Two named things worth having, and where to find them now Garrey's stricture: an ischaemic narrowing of small bowel that has been reduced from an obstructed hernia, found later at operation.​SRB 18 · p.742–743 Pantaloon hernia: lateral and medial hernias present in the same patient.​B&L 64 · p.1067 Where B&L 28e does and does not carry these eponyms. Maydl's and Garrey's (de Garengeot's) are genuinely absent from the whole of the 28th edition: they are S Das and SRB eponyms, so supply them yourself. Amyand's and Littre's are not absent. Both are named in the body text of the paediatric surgery chapter, which says a hernia "may contain omentum, intestine, appendix (Amyand's) or a Meckel's diverticulum (Littre's)".​B&L 17 · p.256 Littre also has the eponym footnote in the hernia chapter.​B&L 64 · p.1080 So if an examiner working from B&L asks for Amyand's, it is in their book, just not in the chapter you were reading.

The modern classification

The European Hernia Society system, which B&L gives as a simplified replacement for the older eponymous systems:​B&L 64 · p.1067

P or R
Primary or recurrent.
L, M or F
Lateral, medial or femoral.
Defect size in fingerbreadths
One fingerbreadth assumed to be 1.5 cm, in three size bands: one fingerbreadth or less; between one and three; three or more.​B&L 64 · p.1067

So a primary, indirect inguinal hernia with a 3 cm defect is PL2.

The named varieties

Sliding hernia (hernia-en-glissade)
Extraperitoneal viscus: caecum on the right, sigmoid on the left, or bladder on either side, slides down outside the sac, forming part of its wall, covered by peritoneum on the hernial aspect only. Older men; reappears slowly after reduction.​Das 38 · p.605 B&L frames it as an acquired indirect hernia arising at the deep ring: retroperitoneal fatty tissue is pushed down the canal first and peritoneum is pulled with it secondarily, so the sac forms second, which is what distinguishes it from a classic indirect hernia. The surgical warning: the bowel may form part of the sac itself and can be damaged during the dissection.​B&L 64 · p.1066
Richter's hernia
Only part of the circumference of the bowel is strangulated. Often complicates a femoral hernia. Treacherous because it mimics gastroenteritis: colic, bowels opening normally, sometimes diarrhoea. Operation is therefore delayed; absolute constipation appears only once paralytic ileus supervenes.​Das 38 · p.605–606 B&L: it may be small and difficult or even impossible to detect clinically, obstruction may or may not be present, and the bowel can still necrose and perforate with life-threatening consequences. Femoral hernia may present in this way, often with diagnostic delay and high risk to the patient.​B&L 64 · p.1060
Littre's hernia
Contains a Meckel's diverticulum.​Das 38 · p.606 SRB's aside worth repeating in viva: Littre described the diverticulum in a hernial sac 81 years before Meckel was born,​SRB 18 · p.743 and B&L prints the same fact in its eponym footnotes.​B&L 64 · p.1080
Amyand's hernia
The appendix in an inguinal hernial sac, often incarcerated.​SRB 18 · p.742
Maydl's hernia (hernia-en-W, retrograde strangulation)
Two loops in the sac, the connecting loop inside the abdomen, where it strangulates first. Suspect it from tenderness above the inguinal ligament with obstruction.​Das 38 · p.606
Interstitial hernia
Arises entirely between the musculofascial layers of the abdominal wall and does not contain a peritoneal sac: commonly seen with small Spigelian hernias. The practical consequence B&L draws is diagnostic: laparoscopy will not identify intraparietal hernias, including lipomas of the spermatic cord and some epigastric and Spigelian hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1062
Internal hernia
Bowel entrapment within the peritoneal cavity: in natural spaces such as the foramen of Winslow and the paraduodenal and paracaecal fossae, around adhesive bands, or through iatrogenic defects in the mesentery.​B&L 64 · p.1061 Not a groin case, but the examiner who asks "what other hernias are there" wants this word.
A misprint to be ready for In the sliding hernia paragraph the 28th edition reads "on the left side, sigmoid colon may descend into a sliding hernia and the caecum may do so on the left".​B&L 64 · p.1067 The second "left" is a misprint: it is the caecum on the right and the sigmoid on the left, as S Das states.​Das 38 · p.605 Learn the anatomy, not the sentence.

Femoral hernia, settled

Boundaries of the femoral canal
Inguinal ligament superoanteriorly, pubic ramus and pectineus inferoposteriorly, lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament medially, femoral vein laterally.​Das 38 · p.606 B&L gives the same four with the posterior wall named as the iliopectineal (Astley Cooper's) ligament, and notes the lacunar ligament is a strong curved ligament with a sharp unyielding edge that impedes reduction.​B&L 64 · p.1071 The space exploited is the one medial to the femoral vein containing fat and the node of Cloquet.​B&L 64 · p.1071
Epidemiology
Rare before 20, peak over 50, commoner in women 2:1, but even in women the commonest groin hernia is the inguinal hernia. Right twice as often as left; bilateral in 20%.​Das 38 · p.606 B&L: the female pelvis has a different shape, increasing the size of the femoral canal and the risk; in old age the defect enlarges further, so femoral hernia is commonly seen in thin, elderly women.​B&L 64 · p.1071
Why it matters
A rigid opening, so it strangulates often: the mirror image of the wide-necked direct hernia that rarely does.​Das 38 · p.604, p.606 B&L's summary box reads: less common than inguinal; more common in women than men; easily missed on examination; 50% present as an emergency with very high risk of strangulation.​B&L 64 · p.1071
Why it is missed, in four specifics
Inadequate exposure of the area; it rapidly becomes irreducible and loses any cough impulse because the neck is tight; it may be only 1–2 cm and is mistaken for a lymph node; and as it enlarges it is reflected superiorly and resembles a direct hernia arising a few centimetres above.​B&L 64 · p.1071
The rule that follows
All patients with unexplained small bowel obstruction should undergo careful examination for a femoral hernia.​B&L 64 · p.1071 And since CT is now commonly done in obstruction, mainly to exclude malignancy, it can identify an obstructing femoral hernia the clinician missed.​B&L 64 · p.1072
There is no conservative option
All femoral hernias should be repaired, and B&L says there is no alternative to surgery and it is wise to treat such cases with some urgency.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1072

7Investigations, and why each one

Which investigation establishes the diagnosis? AnswerNone. For most hernias the diagnosis is made on clinical examination, and most cases of inguinal hernia require no diagnostic tests at all.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1068 Say this first: it reframes everything that follows as investigation for fitness and cause, not for diagnosis.
When they are neededB&L gives three triggers: the patient has symptoms suggesting a hernia but none is found; there is a swelling suggestive of hernia but clinical uncertainty; or more detail is needed than examination can give. And a fourth that is really a caution: be certain the symptoms are due to the hernia and not to coexisting pathology, particularly when the major symptom is pain.​B&L 64 · p.1061

When the diagnosis is genuinely in doubt

Plain abdominal radiograph: of little value
B&L's summary box says so in those words.​B&L 64 · p.1062 The exception is the emergency: in a patient with a femoral hernia presenting acutely, bowel obstruction is often present and a plain radiograph is likely to show it, and that is what should send you back to examine the groin.​B&L 64 · p.1071
Ultrasound: low cost, non-invasive, dynamic, highly operator dependent
For irreducible hernia where the differential includes a mass, fluid collection, enlarged lymph node or saphena varix; when the nature of the content is in doubt; and in the early postoperative period to distinguish a haematoma or seroma from an early recurrence.​B&L 64 · p.1061
CT
Complex and incisional hernia: number and size of defects, content, presence of adhesions, and to exclude other intra-abdominal pathology such as ascites, occult malignancy and portal hypertension. By showing the surrounding muscle layers CT helps planning abdominal wall reconstruction.​B&L 64 · p.1062 Also now common in bowel obstruction, where it can identify an obstructing femoral hernia the clinician missed.​B&L 64 · p.1072
MRI
Best for sportsman's (Gilmore's) groin, where pain is the presenting feature and the surgeon must distinguish an occult hernia from an orthopaedic injury.​B&L 64 · p.1062
Laparoscopy
In inguinal hernia repair by the transabdominal route, initial laparoscopy identifies an occult contralateral hernia; in incisional hernia it determines whether a laparoscopic approach is feasible at all. But it will not identify intraparietal hernias: lipoma of the spermatic cord, some epigastric and Spigelian hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1062
Herniography (Gullmo)
Contrast injected into the peritoneal cavity, films taken supine and prone, to show a sac or asymmetric bulging: especially for an occult inguinal hernia.​SRB 18 · p.741 This one is SRB's, not B&L's: B&L 28e does not list herniography among its investigations, so offer it as the Indian textbook answer and know it has fallen out of the British one.
The trap in cross-sectional imaging Ultrasound, CT and MRI show excellent anatomical detail but may miss groin hernias because they tend to reduce spontaneously in supine patients.​B&L 64 · p.1068 A negative scan does not exclude the hernia you felt. Say that and you have said something most candidates do not.

For the cause, so the repair holds

Chest radiograph, and pulmonary assessment where indicated
Where chronic cough or bronchitis was found. An untreated cough is a pressure load on a fresh repair.​Das 38 · p.595, p.602–603
Prostate and urinary assessment
Where history or rectal examination suggested BPH or stricture. Relieved before or with the repair, and it warns you of postoperative urinary retention.​Das 38 · p.595, p.603​B&L 64 · p.1070
Lower GI evaluation in the older patient with altered bowels
A new hernia with constipation and weight loss raises a colonic cause of straining.

For anaesthesia

Haemoglobin, blood group, blood sugar, urea and creatinine, urinalysis
Baseline fitness; anaemia and uncontrolled diabetes impair wound healing, and the general examination exists partly to select the anaesthetic.​Das 1 · p.8
ECG, chest radiograph by age
In the old or cardiac patient the operation may be done under local anaesthesia.​Das 1 · p.8 B&L: elective surgery for inguinal hernia can be undertaken under local, regional or general anaesthesia with minimal risk, even in high-risk patients.​B&L 64 · p.1068 That single sentence is the answer to "this man is 82 with COPD, would you operate?"
Coagulation screen if anticoagulated
Warfarin, apixaban and antiplatelet agents affect the timing and conduct of surgery.​B&L 64 · p.1061
Say this before anyone asks A strangulated hernia is not investigated into a diagnosis. It is resuscitated and operated on. Time is critical in the presence of ischaemic bowel.​B&L 64 · p.1070 Investigations in that setting are for resuscitation and for the anaesthetist, not for the diagnosis, which you have already made with your hands.

8Treatment, and the reasoning behind each choice

Does this hernia need an operation at all?

Not every hernia does
B&L opens the section with it: an abdominal wall hernia does not necessarily require repair. The patient may ask for surgery for symptoms or for cosmesis. The surgeon should recommend repair when complications are likely, the most worrying being bowel obstruction and strangulation, which are most likely in narrow-necked hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1062
So: always repair
All femoral hernias. Symptomatic or irreducible hernias, unless coexisting medical factors place the patient at very high risk. Increasing difficulty in reduction and increasing size are themselves indications. And surgery should be offered to younger adults, because symptoms and complications are likely over time.​B&L 64 · p.1062
Watchful waiting, and its price
In elderly patients a policy of watchful waiting in an asymptomatic inguinal hernia appears generally safe, with an annual crossover to surgery of around 10% because symptoms develop.​B&L 64 · p.1062 B&L adds the narrower version for inguinal hernia specifically: it is safe to recommend no active treatment in early asymptomatic direct hernia, particularly in elderly patients who do not want surgery, warning them to seek advice if it enlarges or becomes symptomatic.​B&L 64 · p.1068
The truss
Can be used to control a hernia but few surgeons now recommend it, and for inguinal hernia B&L states flatly that surgical trusses are not recommended.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1068
And when conservatism is the braver choice
Large and recurrent incisional hernias: repair is complex with significant risk of complications and later recurrence, and when the neck is wide the risk of strangulation is low, so in obese and elderly patients the risks may outweigh the benefits and a conservative approach is common.​B&L 64 · p.1062
Acute pain in a hernia
Offer urgent surgery. It may reduce by taxis or after admission and analgesia through muscle relaxation, but the likelihood of similar episodes is very high, so operate at that admission or at the next available opportunity.​B&L 64 · p.1062

The principles every repair follows

B&L states them explicitly, and they are worth reciting in order:​B&L 64 · p.1062

1. Reduce the contents
Into the abdominal cavity, with excision of any non-viable tissue and bowel repair if necessary. Reduction of hernia content is essential for a successful repair.
2. Deal with the sac
Excise and close the peritoneal sac if present, though small sacs may be reduced intact. Ideal but not essential. Leaving the sac in situ risks a seroma collecting inside it.
3. Close the defect
If possible. Not always possible when the defect is large, the surrounding tissue rigid (the femoral canal), or a structure must keep traversing it (the cord at the deep ring).
4. Reinforce with mesh
Though non-mesh repairs are an option. Closure of the hernia defect alone is associated with a high recurrence rate, and reinforcement with non-absorbable mesh reduces but does not prevent recurrence.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1063
5. Excise redundant skin if necessary
To improve the cosmetic outcome. New to the printed list, and the kind of item that sounds like you have read the chapter.
How the sac is actually handled, by operation In open repair of a lateral (indirect) hernia most surgeons excise the sac, but small sacs can simply be pushed back through the deep ring, which is said to reduce postoperative pain. In laparoscopic repair the sac is pulled back into the abdomen and not excised at all. In intraperitoneal onlay mesh repair of incisional hernia the sac is often left in situ and a mesh simply fixed over the defect.​B&L 64 · p.1062 If you are asked whether the sac must always come out, the answer is no, and these are the three reasons.

The operations

Herniotomy: excision and closure of the sac alone
Sufficient in children with a lateral hernia and a persistent processus: the wall itself is normal, so removing the sac removes the disease.​B&L 64 · p.1068 SRB gives the anatomical reason: in infants both rings are superimposed with no obliquity of the canal.​SRB 18 · p.743 In adults herniotomy alone has a high recurrence rate and some form of muscle-strengthening repair (herniorrhaphy) is recommended.​B&L 64 · p.1068
Bassini (1890): open suture repair
Open the external oblique aponeurosis, dissect the cord free, confirm lateral or medial. A lateral sac is separated from the cord, opened, contents reduced, the sac sutured closed at its neck and the excess removed. A medial hernia is inverted and the transversalis fascia suture plicated. Sutures then run between the conjoint tendon above and the inguinal ligament below, from pubic tubercle to deep ring, strengthening the posterior wall. It remained the basis of open repair for over 100 years.​B&L 64 · p.1068
Shouldice: the one modification that helped
Over 150 modifications of Bassini have been described with little or no benefit except for Shouldice. The transversalis fascia is opened by a central incision from the deep ring to the pubic tubercle and closed to create a two-layered posterior wall (double breasting); the external oblique is closed in the same way. Expert centres report lifetime failure under 2%, but it is technically demanding and in most hands gives results similar to a Bassini repair.​B&L 64 · p.1068
Maloney darn, and why it matters in India
When a Bassini-type operation is done today, most surgeons use a continuous non-absorbable nylon or polypropylene suture darned between conjoint tendon and inguinal ligament. B&L: "this operation gives excellent results and is the most common operation performed in countries where mesh is too expensive".​B&L 64 · p.1068 Quote that sentence if you are asked to justify a non-mesh repair in a government hospital.
Desarda
A 1–2 cm strip of external oblique aponeurosis lying over the canal is isolated from the main muscle but left attached both medially and laterally, then sutured to conjoint tendon and inguinal ligament. As the abdominal muscles contract the strip tightens, adding physiological support to the posterior wall. The 28th edition now calls it equivalent to a Shouldice repair, where the 26th called it "currently under evaluation".​B&L 64 · p.1068 An Indian operation (Mohan Desarda, Pune) that has been promoted in the British text: worth knowing whose it is.
Lichtenstein: open flat mesh, tension-free
Described in the 1980s; synthetic mesh had been used to reinforce repairs since the 1950s. The first part is identical to Bassini. Then an 8 × 15 cm polypropylene mesh is placed over the posterior wall behind the spermatic cord and slit to wrap around the cord at the deep ring, held with loose sutures to inguinal ligament and conjoint tendon. Two claimed advantages: lower recurrence and faster recovery. What the trials actually show: recurrence within the first 2 years is lower, but acute pain scores are similar. Its commonest complication is chronic pain, reported as high as 20%. It is nevertheless the most common operation for inguinal hernia in resource-rich countries.​B&L 64 · p.1068–1069
Plugs, devices and complex meshes: not recommended
Shaped mesh plugs are simple to insert and need little fixation, but can become solid (meshoma) and migrate or erode into adjacent structures such as the urinary bladder. There is little evidence that any of these techniques is superior to Lichtenstein's operation and their use is not recommended in the 2018 European Hernia Society groin hernia guidelines.​B&L 64 · p.1069 This is firmer than the 26th edition, which only said the evidence was lacking.
Stoppa: open preperitoneal
First described by Annandale in 1880, largely discarded until the 1950s when Stoppa described it with mesh reconstruction through a midline incision. Useful when multiple attempts at open standard surgery have failed and the hernia keeps recurring. Largely superseded by the totally extraperitoneal laparoscopic approach, which is modelled on Stoppa's operation.​B&L 64 · p.1069
Laparoscopic: TEP and TAPP
In both, the hernia and sac are reduced from within and a 10 × 15 cm mesh (or larger) placed in the preperitoneal plane, extending medially into the retropubic space and at least 5 cm lateral to the deep ring, so that it covers Hesselbach's triangle, the deep inguinal ring and the femoral canal: all three at once. In TEP the surgeon develops the extraperitoneal plane without entering the peritoneal cavity. In TAPP the peritoneal cavity is entered first and the peritoneum incised above the defect to open the same space.​B&L 64 · p.1069
Robot-assisted repair
Increasingly used. To date little additional patient benefit has been noted, though the enhanced view and the surgeon's ergonomic comfort are compelling; the cost for a simple inguinal repair remains hard to justify.​B&L 64 · p.1069 New in the 28th edition, and a tidy answer if asked about the future of hernia surgery.
The laparoscopic-versus-open evidence, in one answer Compared with open repair, the laparoscopic approach gives reduced pain both immediately after surgery and up to five years later, more rapid return to full activity, and fewer wound complications such as infection, bleeding and seroma. It is of particular benefit in bilateral hernias and in recurrence after open surgery. The proportion done laparoscopically is slowly rising, but there is a long learning curve.​B&L 64 · p.1069 Note what is not claimed: recurrence is no different between open and laparoscopic.​B&L 64 · p.1070

Mesh: what to say if asked

Three ways to use it
Bridge a defect as a tension-free patch; plug a defect; or augment a repair, closing the defect with sutures and adding mesh for reinforcement. Primary closure plus tension-free mesh reinforcement is currently regarded as optimal.​B&L 64 · p.1063
Overlap, and the one thing never to do
Simple bridging relies on a generous overlap onto strong tissue around the defect. Suturing a mesh edge to edge into the defect (inlay), with no overlap, is not recommended, because it is effectively no more than a suture repair at each mesh-tissue interface.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1065
Net or sheet
Net meshes are woven or knitted and allow native tissue ingrowth between the strands, becoming integrated within a few months; initial fixation is by glue, sutures or tacks, and in some cases, such as extraperitoneal repair of inguinal hernia, no fixation is required at all. Sheet meshes allow no ingrowth, become encapsulated, and always require strong non-absorbable fixation to prevent migration.​B&L 64 · p.1063
Materials
Polypropylene: inert, hydrophobic, monofilament, so it generates no immune response and tends to resist bacterial ingrowth. Polyester: similar but hydrophilic, said to encourage microvascular ingrowth. PTFE: flat sheets, quite inert, resistant to both tissue ingrowth and adhesion formation.​B&L 64 · p.1063
Weight and porosity
Early meshes were over-engineered, stronger than the human abdominal wall itself. All mesh provokes fibrosis; heavyweight mesh provokes more, causing collagen contraction and stiffening, with impaired abdominal wall elasticity, foreign body sensation and pain. Meshes with thinner strands and larger pores are preferred: better integration, less contracture, less foreign body reaction, more flexibility, better comfort. Current opinion avoids stiff heavyweight mesh and favours a pore size of at least 1 mm in all directions, to promote collagen ingrowth that is strong and elastic.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1064
"Shrinkage" is the wrong word
The mesh itself does not shrink. What happens is progressive contraction of the fibrous tissue that has grown into it, so "mesh contracture" is the more accurate term. Meshes can contract in area by more than 50%, which causes tension and pain and leads to recurrence if the mesh no longer covers the defect.​B&L 64 · p.1063
Biological mesh
Sheets of sterilised, decellularised connective tissue from human or animal dermis, bovine pericardium or porcine intestinal submucosa, acting as a scaffold for neovascular ingrowth, fibroblast infiltration and new collagen. In theory host enzymes break the implant down and replace it with normal fibrous tissue. In the presence of infection some break down faster than they remodel, giving early recurrence; cross-linked products resist this. Expensive, and their precise role has yet to be fully established.​B&L 64 · p.1064
Absorbable mesh
Polyglycolic acid, collagen or polyhydroxybutyrate meshes are used for temporary abdominal wall closure and short-term buttressing but are not recommended in hernia repair: they absorb too quickly and induce only minimal collagen. Newer slowly absorbable meshes aim to be replaced by strong native collagen; long-term outcomes are unknown.​B&L 64 · p.1064
Tissue-separating mesh for intraperitoneal use
Two different surfaces, one sticky and one slippery: ingrowth on the parietal side, an anti-adhesive coating of polycellulose, collagen or PTFE on the bowel side. None is 100% effective, so intraperitoneal mesh is associated with bowel obstruction, mesh erosion and fistulation, and surgeons now avoid that plane whenever possible.​B&L 64 · p.1064
Positions, and which are preferred
Onlay (subcutaneous, on top of muscle and fascia) · inlay (within the defect) · sublay (immediately deep to the muscle layers) · extraperitoneal · intraperitoneal. Mesh placed deep to the muscle has a mechanical advantage, because abdominal pressure helps hold it in place: so sublay and extraperitoneal placement are generally preferred. Onlay mesh can be exposed if the wound breaks down, and raising skin flaps for overlap risks skin ischaemia and seroma.​B&L 64 · p.1064, p.1065
Infection, and cost
Infection limits the use of mesh. An infected mesh usually needs to be removed, although some situations can be salvaged with debridement, appropriate antibiotics and modern vacuum-assisted dressings. And the sentence to finish on: price or novelty is not an indicator of quality or safety, and a simple, non-absorbable, large-pore synthetic mesh is nowadays seen as the safest implant.​B&L 64 · p.1065

The strangulated hernia

Resuscitate: nil by mouth, nasogastric tube, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction, catheter, antibiotics
Approximately 5% of inguinal hernias present as an irreducible painful lump that may progress to strangulation and bowel infarction, and time is critical in the presence of ischaemic bowel.​B&L 64 · p.1070
Do not attempt blind taxis on a strangulated hernia
Reducing strangulated bowel returns dead bowel to the abdomen, where perforation goes unwitnessed.​Das 38 · p.600 And if it is reduced, remember Garrey's stricture can follow.​SRB 18 · p.742–743 See the taxis disagreement above for how to phrase this.
The principles of surgery are the same as in the elective setting
Open or laparoscopic is possible depending on local facilities, the surgeon's skills and the patient; B&L no longer states a preference for open, but it notes that it can be very difficult to reduce an incarcerated hernia laparoscopically.​B&L 64 · p.1070
Expect to resect, and plan the incision for it
Approximately 20% of patients presenting as an emergency require bowel resection, which may require conversion to a midline laparotomy, adding significantly to postoperative morbidity and mortality.​B&L 64 · p.1070 This is why, in a femoral hernia with a strangulation risk, the high (McEvedy) approach is chosen: bowel resection is not possible through the low approach, because the completed anastomosis cannot be returned through the narrow femoral canal.​B&L 64 · p.1072
Mesh is still acceptable
Surgical site infection may complicate emergency cases, but unless there is significant infection or contamination, use of synthetic mesh is acceptable as long as the operation is covered by appropriate antibiotics.​B&L 64 · p.1070
Remember Maydl's before you close
The strangulated loop may be the connecting one inside the abdomen.​Das 38 · p.606 B&L does not carry this eponym, so it is yours to supply.

The three open approaches to a femoral hernia

New in detail in the 28th edition, and the single most answerable operative question in a groin case, because the choice follows from one fact: can you resect bowel through it?​B&L 64 · p.1072

ApproachWhat is doneWhen
Low
(Lockwood)		 Transverse incision over the hernia. Sac opened, contents reduced, sac reduced. Non-absorbable sutures between inguinal ligament above and pectineal ligament below. A small cut in the medial lacunar ligament aids reduction, but beware an abnormal branch of the obturator artery just deep to it. Protect the femoral vein laterally. The simplest; can be done under local anaesthesia. Suitable only when there is no risk of bowel resection.
Inguinal
(Lotheissen)		 Incision as for Bassini or Lichtenstein. Cord mobilised, transversalis fascia opened from deep ring to pubic tubercle, entering the extraperitoneal space. The femoral hernia lies immediately below and is reduced by pulling from above and pushing from below. Neck closed with sutures or a plug, protecting the external iliac vein; a mesh may be placed in the canal to prevent a later inguinal hernia. When the inguinal canal needs to be dealt with too.
High
(McEvedy)		 Most surgeons now use the Nyhus modification: a transverse incision just above the inguinal canal on the lateral border of rectus. Anterior rectus sheath incised, muscle retracted, preperitoneal space entered. Hernia reduced, sac opened, contents inspected; in dubious cases the bowel is replaced in the abdomen for 5 minutes and re-examined. Defect closed with sutures or mesh. Ideal in the emergency where strangulation risk is high. Needs regional or general anaesthesia. Allows a generous peritoneal incision, so bowel resection is feasible. Can be extended to repair bilateral femoral hernias through one incision (Henry).

Whole table: Bailey & Love ch.64, p.1072.

And in women, laparoscopic B&L recommends the laparoscopic approach for femoral hernia in women, because of the increased early recurrence observed in women, thought to relate more to misdiagnosis of the hernia, inguinal versus femoral, than to true recurrence. Laparoscopy visualises all the hernia orifices at once and removes the diagnostic uncertainty.​B&L 64 · p.1072 That is a clean, modern answer to "why laparoscopy for a groin hernia in a woman?"
