Complications of hernia surgery

TimingComplicationDetail
EarlyBleeding or haematoma Usually from subcutaneous vessels, occasionally from accidental damage to the inferior epigastric or iliac vessels.
Urinary retentionMay require catheterisation. Prostatic symptoms in the history are your warning.
Femoral nerve blockade From infusion of local anaesthetic; the patient cannot move the leg. Resolves over some hours but is alarming if you have not warned anyone.
First weekPain, bruising, swellingCommon, and expected.
Seroma An inflammatory response to dissection, sutures or mesh; more common if the peritoneal sac is left in situ. Usually resolves spontaneously, sometimes aspirated. After laparoscopic surgery it may be misdiagnosed as early recurrence.
Wound infection Less frequent than pain and bruising. Despite the potential for contamination of a groin incision and the use of mesh, routine antibiotics are not recommended in recent guidelines.
LateChronic pain Pain persisting more than three months. Common after all forms of surgery and possibly affects as many as 20% after groin hernia repair. Less common and less severe after laparoscopic surgery. The most severe is neuralgic, from nerve injury at operation or chronic irritation by suture or mesh.
Recurrence No operation can be guaranteed recurrence free; good centres aim for a 5-year recurrence rate of less than 5%. Mesh beats suture, but there is no difference between mesh repairs and none between open and laparoscopic. There is very strong evidence that specialist hernia surgeons have lower recurrence and lower chronic pain rates whatever technique they use.
Testicular infarction Rare, from damage to the testicular artery: perhaps the most serious complication in a young man. There is no evidence that hernia surgery affects male fertility, despite extensive study.

Whole table: Bailey & Love ch.64, p.1070. Its own summary box compresses it to: early, pain, bleeding and haematoma, urinary retention; medium, seroma and wound infection; late, chronic pain and testicular atrophy.

Who gets chronic pain, and how to avoid causing it Higher risk: females, the young, those whose hernia was painful beforehand, those with a pre-existing chronic pain syndrome, those with an exaggerated response to a heat stimulus, and those with certain psychological tendencies. What the surgeon controls: the handling of the three nerves in the inguinal canal, the ilioinguinal, the iliohypogastric and the genital branch of the genitofemoral. Allow for anatomical variation, keep each nerve within its connective tissue surroundings where possible, and if a nerve has to be sacrificed, divide it as proximally as practicable and bury the end in the muscle belly. In laparoscopic surgery, avoid placing sutures, staples or tacks in the retroperitoneal area. Chronic pain is uncommon after laparoscopic repair precisely because the work is done at a deeper level, away from these nerves.​B&L 64 · p.1066, p.1070

9Rapid-fire viva

What are the two classical signs of an uncomplicated hernia, and what are the two caveats?

Impulse on coughing and reducibility.​Das 38 · p.598 Caveats, which Bailey & Love prints as its own summary box: a swelling with a cough impulse is not necessarily a hernia, and a swelling with no cough impulse may still be a hernia, though you should then consider other diagnoses.​B&L 64 · p.1061

Is a hernia caused by heavy lifting?

The classical answer is yes: straining, cough, constipation and bladder outflow obstruction.​SRB 18 · p.740 But Bailey & Love 28e begins from the premise that a normal abdominal wall has sufficient strength to resist high pressure, so the strain brings the hernia to the patient's attention rather than causing it. The evidence favours an inherited imbalance of collagen types, supported by histology, by the association with aortic aneurysm, by the difficulty of repair in Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, and by the fact that smoking raises risk through impaired collagen maturation.​B&L 64 · p.1060 SRB agrees in its own words, calling acquired herniation a collagen deficiency, metastatic emphysema of Read.​SRB 18 · p.741

Give B&L's six causes of hernia in order.

Anatomical weakness; developmental failures; genetic weakness of collagen; sharp and blunt trauma; weakness due to ageing and pregnancy; primary neurological and muscle diseases.​B&L 64 · p.1059

What are the only natural weaknesses of the abdominal wall, and what makes the rest?

The only weaknesses from inadequate muscular strength are the lumbar triangles and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Everything else is where a structure enters or leaves: the inguinal canal for the testis or round ligament, the oesophageal hiatus, the femoral canal and the umbilical cicatrix.​B&L 64 · p.1059

Why does an incisional hernia happen, and how often?

A surgical scar, even with perfect healing, has only 70% of the initial muscle strength. At least 10% of laparotomy incisions herniate; laparoscopic port sites, 1%. Incisional hernia is also more common after wound complications and with a high BMI, and a major risk factor is the surgeon and the way the wall was closed.​B&L 64 · p.1059, p.1060

Define incarcerated. How does it differ from irreducible and from strangulated?

Incarcerated, literally "in prison", means the hernia is not only irreducible but also potentially developing strangulation: the stage between the two. Irreducible means the contents will not return but the blood supply is intact and nothing else is wrong; strangulated means the blood supply has been arrested. Beyond strangulated, B&L adds infarcted, where the contents are gangrenous, with high mortality.​B&L 64 · p.1060 S Das and SRB do not use incarcerated as a separate clinical type.​Das 38 · p.604–605

Why can a small hernia be more dangerous than a large one?

Because the risk follows the defect, not the lump. A small defect with rigid walls traps the content, preventing it moving freely in and out; the narrow neck then acts as a constriction ring, impeding venous return, raising pressure, and progressing from irreducibility to strangulation. A wide-necked hernia, such as a direct inguinal or a large incisional hernia, rarely strangulates. B&L prints it as a management rule: small hernias can be more dangerous than large.​B&L 64 · p.1060, p.1062

Which hernias must always be repaired?

All femoral hernias, because the opening is rigid and 50% present as an emergency. Also symptomatic or irreducible hernias unless the patient is at very high medical risk, hernias becoming harder to reduce or larger, and hernias in younger adults because symptoms and complications are likely over time.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1071

Is watchful waiting ever acceptable in an inguinal hernia?

Yes. In elderly patients a policy of watchful waiting in an asymptomatic inguinal hernia appears generally safe, with an annual crossover to surgery of around 10% as symptoms develop; it is specifically safe in an early asymptomatic direct hernia in an elderly patient who does not want an operation, provided he is warned to return if it enlarges or becomes symptomatic. Surgical trusses are not recommended.​B&L 64 · p.1062, p.1068

Where is the deep inguinal ring?

The answer your examiner wants: half an inch above the mid-inguinal point, midway between the ASIS and the symphysis pubis.​Das 38 · p.599​SRB 18 · p.743 Bailey & Love places it midway between the ASIS and the pubic tubercle, the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, about 2–3 cm above and marginally lateral to the femoral artery pulse.​B&L 64 · p.1065 The two points are about 1–1.5 cm apart: the mid-inguinal point overlies the femoral artery, the midpoint of the inguinal ligament overlies the deep ring. Give the S Das answer and state the distinction if pressed.

Recite the four principles of hernia repair. B&L 28e has five.

Reduce the contents, excising non-viable tissue and repairing bowel if necessary; excise and close the peritoneal sac if present, though small sacs may be reduced intact; close the defect if possible; reinforce with mesh, since closure alone has a high recurrence rate; and, fifth in the 28th edition, excise redundant skin if necessary for cosmesis.​B&L 64 · p.1062

Must the sac always be excised?

No. Excision and closure is ideal but not essential. In open repair of a lateral hernia most surgeons excise it, but a small sac can be pushed back through the deep ring, which is said to reduce postoperative pain. In laparoscopic repair the sac is pulled back into the abdomen and not excised. In intraperitoneal onlay mesh repair of an incisional hernia the sac is often left in situ. The price of leaving it is seroma formation inside it.​B&L 64 · p.1062

Describe the Shouldice repair and how it differs from Bassini.

Bassini, 1890, sutures conjoint tendon to inguinal ligament from pubic tubercle to deep ring, strengthening the posterior wall; it was the basis of open repair for over 100 years. Shouldice first opens the transversalis fascia by a central incision from deep ring to pubic tubercle and closes it as a two-layered posterior wall, double breasting, then closes the external oblique the same way. Of over 150 modifications of Bassini it is the only one with benefit; under 2% lifetime failure in expert centres, but technically demanding and in most hands no better than Bassini.​B&L 64 · p.1068

In a hospital that cannot afford mesh, what do you do, and can you defend it?

A Maloney darn: a continuous non-absorbable nylon or polypropylene suture darned between conjoint tendon and inguinal ligament, which is how most Bassini-type operations are now done. Bailey & Love itself says this operation gives excellent results and is the most common operation performed in countries where mesh is too expensive. Desarda's repair, using a strip of external oblique aponeurosis left attached at both ends so it tightens as the muscles contract, is a second mesh-free option and the 28th edition now rates it equivalent to Shouldice.​B&L 64 · p.1068

What size mesh, and what does it have to cover?

Lichtenstein: 8 × 15 cm over the posterior wall behind the cord, slit to wrap around the cord at the deep ring. Laparoscopic TEP or TAPP: 10 × 15 cm or larger in the preperitoneal plane, extending medially into the retropubic space and at least 5 cm lateral to the deep ring, covering Hesselbach's triangle, the deep inguinal ring and the femoral canal together. General rule for any bridging mesh: a generous overlap onto strong tissue; inlay, edge to edge with no overlap, is not recommended.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1068, p.1069

Why are large-pore, lightweight meshes preferred?

Better tissue integration, less contracture, less foreign body reaction, more flexibility and better comfort. Heavyweight mesh provokes a greater fibrous reaction, with collagen contraction and stiffening, impaired abdominal wall mobility, foreign body sensation and pain. Current opinion avoids stiff heavyweight mesh and favours a pore size of at least 1 mm in all directions, so the ingrowth is strong and also elastic. Note the 28th edition drops the old weight thresholds in g/m² and argues from pore size instead.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1064

What is meshoma, and what is the current advice on mesh plugs?

A solid fibrous mass formed by collagen deposition in a mesh plug, which may cause chronic pain; plugs can also migrate and erode into adjacent organs such as the bladder, and cause fistulas. Plug repairs have been largely abandoned, there is little evidence that any plug or device is superior to Lichtenstein's operation, and their use is not recommended in the 2018 European Hernia Society groin hernia guidelines.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1069

A mesh gets infected. What happens?

It usually has to be removed, though some cases can be salvaged with debridement, appropriate antibiotics and vacuum-assisted dressings. Polypropylene, being hydrophobic and monofilament, tends to resist bacterial ingrowth; polyester is hydrophilic. In emergency surgery, unless there is significant infection or contamination, synthetic mesh is still acceptable under antibiotic cover.​B&L 64 · p.1063, p.1065, p.1070

Compare laparoscopic and open inguinal hernia repair.

Laparoscopic gives less pain immediately and up to five years later, faster return to full activity and fewer wound complications: infection, bleeding, seroma. It is of particular benefit in bilateral hernias and in recurrence after open surgery. Recurrence is no different between the two, nor between mesh types. The limitation is a long learning curve. Robot assistance adds little patient benefit so far and is hard to justify on cost for a simple repair.​B&L 64 · p.1069, p.1070

Your patient has had a Lichtenstein repair and has groin pain four months later. What is it?

Chronic pain, defined as pain persisting more than three months after surgery, and the commonest complication of open flat mesh repair, possibly affecting as many as 20% of patients after groin hernia repair. The most severe form is neuralgic, from injury to or chronic irritation of the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric or genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve by suture material or mesh, or from mesh contracture causing tissue tension. It is less common and less severe after laparoscopic repair.​B&L 64 · p.1069, p.1070

How would you reduce the risk of chronic pain at operation?

Identify and protect the three nerves of the inguinal canal, allowing for anatomical variation and keeping each within its connective tissue surroundings. If a nerve must be sacrificed, divide it as proximally as practicable and bury the end in the muscle belly. In laparoscopic repair, avoid putting sutures, staples or tacks into the retroperitoneal area. And recognise the patients at higher risk beforehand: women, the young, a hernia that was painful before surgery, a pre-existing chronic pain syndrome, an exaggerated response to heat stimulus, certain psychological tendencies.​B&L 64 · p.1066, p.1070

Why is rectal examination obligatory in a case of hernia?

To exclude chronic constipation and an enlarged prostate, causes of straining that will recur the hernia if untreated; the word in S Das is obligatory.​Das 38 · p.603 It also warns you of postoperative urinary retention, which is one of B&L's immediate complications of inguinal hernia surgery.​B&L 64 · p.1070

A patient has unexplained small bowel obstruction. What must you do?

Examine the groins carefully for a femoral hernia: all patients with unexplained small bowel obstruction should undergo careful examination for one. It is easily missed because the area is inadequately exposed, it rapidly becomes irreducible and loses its cough impulse, it may be only 1–2 cm and is mistaken for a lymph node, and once large it is reflected superiorly and mimics a direct hernia. CT is now commonly performed in obstruction and can identify a femoral hernia the clinician missed.​B&L 64 · p.1071, p.1072

You are operating on a strangulated femoral hernia. Which approach, and why?

The high (McEvedy) approach, now usually in the Nyhus modification: a transverse incision just above the inguinal canal on the lateral border of rectus, through the anterior rectus sheath into the preperitoneal space. It is ideal in the emergency because it allows a generous peritoneal incision, so the bowel can be inspected and resected. The low (Lockwood) approach cannot be used if resection is a possibility, because the completed anastomosis cannot be returned to the abdomen through the narrow femoral canal. In doubtful bowel, replace it in the abdomen for 5 minutes and look again. About 20% of emergency presentations need a bowel resection.​B&L 64 · p.1070, p.1072

How confident can you be in distinguishing direct from indirect at the bedside?

Honestly, not very. Bailey & Love states that even experienced surgeons find it difficult to distinguish lateral and medial hernias with certainty.​B&L 64 · p.1067 Use the ring occlusion and invagination tests, state your best answer, and acknowledge that the definitive distinction is made at operation.

Something moves down the inguinal canal on coughing. Is it a hernia?

Not necessarily: movement is not a criterion. An encysted hydrocele of the cord or an undescended testis can do the same. Look for an expansile impulse and use the traction test: pulling the testis down makes an encysted hydrocele of the cord descend slightly and become fixed.​Das 38 · p.599, p.601–602 A saphena varix also gives a definite cough impulse, increases on standing and is misdiagnosed as a hernia, particularly in pregnant women.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1067

In a child with a suspected hernia and nothing visible, what do you do?

Make him jolt, jump off the table, or cry, then palpate the cord at the superficial ring: it feels thicker than the other side because of the sac. If that fails, Cornall's test: hold the child from behind with both hands on the abdomen, press and lift him up.​Das 38 · p.601 And remember the principle: inguinal hernia in neonates and children is always the congenital type.​B&L 64 · p.1066

Would you repair the other side as well?

Occult contralateral hernias are present in up to 20% of patients, and a patient with a single hernia has a 50% lifetime risk of developing one on the other side, so the other groin must always be examined. Some surgeons have suggested offering bilateral repair, especially if laparoscopic surgery is planned, but that is not widespread practice at present.​B&L 64 · p.1061, p.1067 Note the figure: the 26th edition said a 33% lifetime risk, the 28th says 50%.

Why is the standing examination not optional?

A direct hernia disappears the moment the patient lies down.​Das 38 · p.596, p.604 B&L examines lying first and then standing, because standing usually increases hernia size and some hernias are apparent only standing; the patient may also be asked to cough or to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre.​B&L 64 · p.1061 So: standing to demonstrate, supine to reduce and assess the defect.

Name a hernia that contains no peritoneal sac.

An interstitial hernia, which arises entirely between the musculofascial layers of the wall, commonly a small Spigelian hernia. Many epigastric hernias also begin without a sac, in the interstitial layers, drawing peritoneum in only secondarily as they enlarge. The clinical consequence is that laparoscopy will not identify intraparietal hernias, including lipoma of the spermatic cord and some epigastric and Spigelian hernias.​B&L 64 · p.1058, p.1061, p.1062 SRB makes the same point about the epigastric hernia having no sac.​SRB 18 · p.741

What is an internal hernia?

Bowel entrapment within the peritoneal cavity: in naturally existing spaces such as the foramen of Winslow or the paraduodenal and paracaecal fossae, around adhesive bands, or through iatrogenic defects in the mesentery.​B&L 64 · p.1061

Is divarication of the recti a hernia?

No. It is lateral stretching of the linea alba as the two rectus muscles separate, predominantly in the upper abdomen in middle-aged overweight men and below the umbilicus after pregnancy in women. It is not a hernia and does not require treatment, although some surgeons offer repair for purely cosmetic reasons. It is best seen by asking a supine patient to lift the head off the pillow.​B&L 64 · p.1058, p.1061

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page so they can be found in a different edition. Where the books disagree, both positions are given and the amber boxes say which to answer. Note that the 28th edition of Bailey & Love renumbered every chapter: hernia is now chapter 64, where the 26th edition had it at chapter 60. Several figures and claims changed with it, and the amber boxes say where.
